title: Strength in weakness (2 Corinthians 12:10)
hook: when I am weak, then I am strong

segments.voice: Yesterday, unanswered prayer: Paul asked three times for the thorn to go, and heard, my grace is sufficient. Your line was my grace is sufficient. When did your thorn press, and what carried you? Day one thousand three hundred ninety.

Paul had critics in Corinth, and he quotes them in his own letter. His letters, they say, are "weighty and powerful; but his bodily presence is weak, and his speech contemptible." Strong on paper, unimpressive in person. The obvious reply to a review like that is a list of achievements. Paul starts to, then turns it upside down. Instead of hiding his weak points, he puts them on display: the beatings, the shipwrecks, the sleepless nights, the thorn. And then he writes a line that turns the whole review around. Today: strength in weakness.
screen: `HE PUTS HIS WEAK POINTS ON DISPLAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the line, right after the thorn: "Therefore I take pleasure in infirmities, in reproaches, in necessities, in persecutions, in distresses for Christ's sake: for when I am weak, then am I strong." First, notice the word therefore. It follows straight from yesterday's answer, my strength is made perfect in weakness. Paul isn't saying weakness is good in itself. He's saying it's the place where a strength not his own shows up. Just before, he writes, "Most gladly therefore will I rather glory in my infirmities, that the power of Christ may rest upon me." Second, a picture from earlier in the same letter: "But we have this treasure in earthen vessels, that the excellency of the power may be of God, and not of us." Clay jars. Cheap, breakable, ordinary kitchen pottery, holding treasure. If the jar were gold, you'd admire the jar. Because it's clay, you notice what's inside. Third, this isn't only Paul's private mood. To the same church he wrote earlier, "God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty." Some readers think of a shepherd boy, fishermen, a carpenter's son: people nobody expected much from. Last, what it does not mean. It doesn't mean staying in harm, or calling cruelty a blessing, or pretending pain is pleasant. Paul's list is hardship for Christ's sake, not abuse to be endured in silence. The point is honesty: when you stop pretending to be strong, there's room for help: from God, in Paul's telling, and from people. Weak, then strong.

Here's the practice: admit one weakness. Settle, and breathe. Name one place where you're not strong right now. Not a humble-brag, a real one: patience that runs out, a fear, something you can't do, help you need. Say it plainly to yourself, in one sentence, without apologizing for it. Then picture a clay jar in your hands, ordinary and a little chipped. If you pray, you can offer the weakness to God and ask for strength that isn't yours. If you don't, notice what it's like to stop pretending. The bell holds the time.
Strength in weakness. Paul's discovery that when he stopped hiding his limits, a power not his own could rest on him: treasure in clay jars.
Your line: weak, then strong. Today, tell one person about the weakness you named, and ask for the help you need. Day one thousand three hundred ninety.

howItsDone: Some Christians turn to 2 Corinthians 12 in illness, addiction recovery and hard seasons, and some churches and recovery groups speak openly about weakness and dependence on God and on one another rather than hiding them.

fork.setup: you're Paul. critics say you're weak and unimpressive in person. how do you answer them?
options: list your achievements and prove them wrong.
fork.reveal: Paul boasts in his infirmities, so that the power of Christ may rest on him: when I am weak, then am I strong.

original.note: Greek: weakness, infirmity, the word behind "my strength is made perfect in weakness."

trapdoor: what you thought: strength in weakness is a nice way of saying try harder.
what it means: Paul stops hiding his limits, and finds a strength not his own resting on him.
what a scholar hears: the word for weakness, astheneia, is also used for illness. Paul's boast turns the critics' word against them: the weak presence is where the power shows.
recall: Catholic and Orthodox word for it

notes: Hook summarizes Paul's hardship list (beatings, shipwrecks, sleepless nights) from 2 Corinthians 11:23–27 without counts. Confirm.
'Shepherd boys, fishermen, a carpenter's son' illustrates 1 Corinthians 1:27 with David, the disciples and Jesus; Paul does not name them there. Confirm.
The caution that strength in weakness does not mean enduring abuse is the writer's pastoral framing; confirm wording.
Trapdoor: astheneia also used for illness: lexical claim. Confirm.
